verifyAudit.subtitle: Paste a CID anchored by Nirium's Audit Trail Node and independently confirm what it declares, when it was anchored, and, if the record was recomputed and compared (not just displayed), whether it still matches.
verifyAudit.scope_note: This is a single-record lookup, not a public feed of every anchor: a CID someone anchored for their own evidence (a third party's audit package, for example) isn't meant for open browsing, so it's only shown when you already have its CID.
verifyAudit.proves_title: What a receipt proves that the ledger doesn't
ledger_items: Who paid whom, which asset and how much
That the payer authorized it (their signature)
That it settled, in which ledger and at what time
That nobody can change it afterwards
A short reference, if the payment carries a memo (up to 28 characters or a hash)
receipt_items: What doesn't fit in a memo: "0.02 USDC paid for GET /signals, request r-123, response delivered"
A payment that never happened: if a policy refuses a $25 charge, there is no transaction; the decision can be anchored as a receipt
Records that never touch the chain: a partner's exchange-rate quote, the evidence behind an escrow release, the invoice or order being paid, or which version of the terms a user accepted
Private evidence: only its hash is public; the file stays with you, and anyone you give it to can check it matches
Who stands behind it: signed with the declarer's own Stellar key, so anyone can check the signer said it, not Nirium, and any later change shows
verifyAudit.proves_footer: If all you need to prove is the transfer, link the transaction. A receipt shows a record hasn't changed since it was anchored; it doesn't prove the record is true.
planned_items: Anchors on Stellar itself: each batch of receipts gets one Merkle root in a Soroban contract, so a receipt can be proven from Stellar alone and its time comes from the ledger, not our server clock

Policy-decision receipts built in: every ALLOW or DENY from the pre-sign hook anchored automatically, including payments that were refused and never signed (AgentLedger already anchors its own decisions by hand)
One receipt format for Stellar payments, x402 payments and escrow releases
Reconciliation that flags a payment with no receipt, or a receipt with no payment
verifyAudit.planned_footer: None of this is live yet. Everything above this box works today.
verifyAudit.example_note: Nirium's test anchor is our own mainnet self-test. The quote is signed with TIA's own key on mainnet: a record that never touches the chain. The payment receipt is a Nirium self-test on testnet: its record only repeats the transaction, which is why the transaction itself is the proof of the payment. The payment that never happened is AgentLedger's own receipt, on mainnet, for a payment its policy blocked: there is no transaction, so the receipt is the only record of the decision.
verifyAudit.searching_title: Looking up this CID on IPFS…
verifyAudit.searching_hint: Gateway propagation can take 60 to 90 seconds right after anchoring. Retrying automatically (attempt {attempt}/{max}).
verifyAudit.error_invalid_cid: That doesn't look like a CID. Paste the bare CID (Qm… or bafy…) or a full gateway URL containing /ipfs/.
verifyAudit.error_not_found: Could not reach this record on the IPFS gateway after several attempts. It may still be propagating, or the CID may not exist.
verifyAudit.error_not_audit_doc: This CID resolved, but its content doesn't look like a Nirium audit record: no `content_sha256` field was found.
verifyAudit.error_generic: Something went wrong reading this record. Please try again.

result.verdict_mismatch: Record does NOT match the declared hash
result.verdict_no_record: Anchor found, no embedded record to recompute
result.tx_note: The payment itself is proven by this transaction on Stellar.
result.no_record_note: This anchor only declares a hash. The original evidence lives with whoever anchored it, not inside this document. There is nothing embedded here to recompute; if you have that evidence, compare it below without uploading it.
result.attestation_valid: Signature verified: this key did sign this exact hash
result.attestation_invalid: Signature does NOT verify. Do not trust this attribution
result.signer_no_account: This key only signs: it has no account or funds on the network. The signature is still valid.
result.attestation_none: No agent attestation on this record. The CID still proves the content wasn't altered after anchoring; it just doesn't prove who anchored it.

codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.title: Código 402: the agents that pay - a free Stellar bootcamp
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.excerpt: Your code has never charged you a dime. A free, 5-session bootcamp with BAF, on Stellar, where you build an API that charges per call and an agent that pays on its own, on Stellar testnet.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.h1: Your code has never charged you a dime. This changes that.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.hook: Every time an AI agent calls your API and you don't charge it, you paid for it - the compute, the inference, the bandwidth. Free. Forever, until now.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_curiosity: HTTP 402 - "Payment Required" - was reserved "for future use" in 1997, and it almost never got used. Until now.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_why1: Until recently, the internet only knew how to charge humans: cards, subscriptions, checkouts. An AI agent doesn't have a card, doesn't open a cart, doesn't wait 3 days for an invoice to get approved. It needs to pay the instant it decides to use something, with no person watching.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_why2: x402 is the protocol that finally solves that: an agent calls your API, your API answers "402, this costs 0.02 USDC", the agent pays right there, and gets its response in seconds. No account, no contract, no friction. It's already happening on mainnet.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.who_dev_body: You leave with a real repo: an API that charges, an agent that pays, and a verifiable receipt. Not notes - running code.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.who_nondev_body: No session assumes you already know blockchain. If you follow basic logic, you'll understand every step - and see firsthand where the agent-run internet is headed.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.step1_body: 0.02 USDC before it answers a single request. No card, no invoice, no human in the loop.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.step2_body: on its own, inside a spending limit you set. Nobody approves each payment by hand.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.step3_body: signed and anchored, that anyone can verify - no one, including us, can fake it.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_risk: 100% on Stellar testnet. Test money, zero real risk. If you break something, nothing happens - that's the point of a sandbox.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_identity: If you already know how to code - basic JavaScript, no blockchain background needed - you can do this. You don't leave with notes. You leave with your own public repo, working.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.h_learn: What you'll actually learn, session by session
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.learn1: How a Stellar payment works end to end, with no middlemen
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.learn2: How to make any endpoint in your API charge per use, with the x402 protocol
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.learn3: How to give an AI agent a spending limit it can't go around
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.learn4: How to anchor a receipt anyone can verify, without trusting you
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.learn5: How to read and check a payment directly on the network, without a third-party dashboard
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.p_sessions: First Stellar payment. Charging for an API with x402. An agent that pays on its own, inside a spending limit it cannot go around. Verifying a payment via RPC or Horizon, with Nirium as the real case study. And a Demo Day where you show what you shipped.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.build1_title: An API that pays for itself
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.build1_body: Any service of yours - data, compute, your own model - billed per call, no Stripe, no monthly plan.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.build2_body: A bot that finds the best price, pays, and delivers the result - with no human approving each transaction.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.build3_body: Agents buying and selling services from other agents, 24/7, with no office or schedule.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.build4_body: Receipts a client can check themselves, instead of just taking your word for it.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.where_body: Hosted by the Blockchain Acceleration Foundation, taught with Nirium - payment and audit-trail infrastructure for AI agents that has settled real x402 payments on Stellar mainnet (latest: 29 Sep 2026).
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.roadmap_body: A Soroban contract that batches these receipts into a single verifiable anchor. Not built yet - it is part of our roadmap.
codigo-402-agentes-que-pagan.verify_body: You do not have to take our word for it. Check a real receipt right now.

audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.title: Anchor a receipt signed with your own Stellar key
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Hash it, sign it with a Stellar key, POST it, and get a CID that anyone can check. Free during the beta.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.h1: Anchor a receipt signed with your own Stellar key
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.p1: An agent acts. An agent pays. Later, someone asks who did what, and when. If the only answer lives in your own database, you are asking people to trust you.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.p2: Audit Trail gives you another answer. You anchor a fingerprint of the evidence to IPFS and sign it with a Stellar key. Anyone can check it without asking us.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step1_p: Take the bytes you want to be able to prove later and compute their sha-256. The evidence itself stays with you.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step2_p: Sign the exact text nirium-audit-v1:<sha-256> with your Stellar key. A Stellar G address is an ed25519 public key, so any Stellar key pair works. The prefix stops a signature made for something else from being reused here.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step3_p: Send the hash and the signature to POST /api/audit/log. The box checks the signature. If it is wrong, it answers 400 and anchors nothing. If it is right, it pins a small document to IPFS and returns its CID.

audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p3: The box answered 201 with a CID:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p4: The document it pinned is public. This is what the CID returns:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p5: We also sent a request signed by a different key than the one it claimed. The box answered 400, with an error that names the exact text to sign, and anchored nothing.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.evidence_doc_label: The anchored document from this run
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p1: You do not need to trust the box. You need the CID and your original evidence. This script downloads the document, recomputes the sha-256, rebuilds the signed text and checks the ed25519 signature against the G key.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p2: This is the output of the real run, with the right evidence:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p3: We also changed one word of the evidence, from approved to rejected. The hash check printed false and the script exited with an error. Run it with your own CID and your own evidence.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.h_limits: What it proves and what it does not
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit1_p: The document has not changed since it was pinned, because its CID comes from its content. The hash matches your evidence. The holder of the G key signed that hash.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit2_p: It does not prove that the content is true. It does not say who is behind a G key in real life. The anchoredAt field is the time the box wrote into the document, not an independent timestamp.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit3_p: IPFS records cannot be deleted. Anchor the hash of your evidence. The optional record field is capped at 8KB, and you are responsible for what you put in it.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit4_p: Free during the beta and rate-limited. The box sets the network, not the request: it anchors on whichever network it runs on, mainnet or testnet, never the one the client asks for.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.mainnet_p1: We ran the exact flow above against the mainnet box too, with a separate throwaway key and this evidence: {"action":"approved","ref":"demo-receipt-mainnet-001"}. It anchored the same way: 201, a CID, a document that verifies.

audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Run the two scripts with a key of your own. Start with GET /api/audit/info, which lists the current rules.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.where_body: GET /api/audit/info lists the rules, the limits and the two endpoints. POST /api/audit/log anchors a hash.

bbva-open-deal-room.title: Nirium at The Open Deal Room by Stellar - BBVA Tower, Mexico City
bbva-open-deal-room.excerpt: We were one of six Stellar startups featured at La Arena inside BBVA Tower CDMX. Here is what we showed, who was in the room, and why an autonomous treasury agent belongs in front of institutional investors.
bbva-open-deal-room.h1: Nirium at The Open Deal Room by Stellar
bbva-open-deal-room.p1: On May 21, 2026, Nirium was featured at The Open Deal Room by Stellar, hosted inside BBVA Tower in Mexico City. We were one of six Stellar ecosystem startups invited to La Arena - a curated room where builders present in front of venture investors, angels, and institutional players active in the Mexican fintech landscape.
bbva-open-deal-room.p2: It is not every day that an autonomous, on-chain treasury agent gets to stand in the lobby of one of Latin America's largest banks. That contrast is exactly the point.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_hook_quote: As a founder, I was my own treasurer - and I slept. So did the money.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_problem: We opened with a problem every Mexican founder feels: corporate cash sits idle. It loses roughly 10% a year to inflation while it sleeps in an account, and keeping it productive is a 24/7 manual job nobody has time for.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_solution: Then the turn - Nirium wakes the money that sleeps. An autonomous agent moves idle USDC into CETES, Mexican sovereign debt, through Etherfuse, and back to liquid the moment it is needed: instantly, and without a treasury desk.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_team: We closed on the team: Giovanny Amador (Founder) and Monserrat Mendoza (Co-founder). A team that has already shipped together.
bbva-open-deal-room.presented_p1: We walked the room through the core of Nirium: a non-custodial agent that moves idle corporate USDC into Mexican government bonds (CETES) through Etherfuse, designed to run around the clock, with a Soroban contract enforcing every transfer.
bbva-open-deal-room.presented_p2: The message we kept returning to is the security pattern that makes this safe to put in front of institutions. An AI agent can read the market and propose a rebalance, but it never holds custody - a Soroban vault (NiriumVault, on testnet) enforces delegation scopes on-chain, so a compromised or hallucinating agent physically cannot move funds the contract did not authorize. (Corrected 12 Nov 2026: this post first called NiriumVault a 2-of-3 multisig. The contract supports a 2-of-3 emergency pause, with no cosigners registered yet; a withdrawal needs only the owner's signature.)
bbva-open-deal-room.pattern_quote: The LLM proposes, the contract decides.
bbva-open-deal-room.venue_p1: Tokenized real-world assets in Mexico are no longer a thesis on a slide. CETES on Stellar via an independent operator is a live corridor, and seeing it discussed inside BBVA Tower - rather than a hackathon side room - signals how quickly institutional appetite is forming. Nirium's position is deliberately software-only and non-custodial: independent third parties handle settlement, while we provide the rails developers and fintechs embed.
bbva-open-deal-room.takeaway_p1: Beyond the pitch, the value of La Arena was the conversations it opened - with investors and ecosystem operators who understand both the Stellar stack and the Mexican regulatory context. Those are the relationships that turn a working testnet protocol into a funded, audited, mainnet product. We left with new threads to pull, and a clearer read on what institutional partners need to see next: verifiable adoption, not promises.
bbva-open-deal-room.where_body: Nirium runs an autonomous agent on Stellar testnet and published TypeScript and Python SDKs. On mainnet, x402 payments, Audit Trail and Reporting already run, receive-only and non-custodial; MPP is experimental. NiriumVault, our own treasury contract, remains audit-gated. Backed by the Stellar ecosystem: two-time Stellar Community Fund Instawards recipient (via the Stellar Ambassador Program) and an active Stellar Mexico Ambassador. Updated 16 Nov 2026: 'regulated' now reads 'independent' where this post described Etherfuse and other third parties, because we have not checked their regulatory status ourselves. The product also changed since May: today the Treasury node moves a vault's funds into the vault's own strategy and back, one asset per vault, and does not convert USDC into CETES.

treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.title: The Treasury Node on Mainnet: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Contract
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Nirium's agent holds the RebalanceManager role on a real DeFindex vault on Stellar mainnet - and the vault's own contract code makes withdrawal structurally impossible for that role, not just against our policy. Here is the transaction, the exact line of source code that proves it, and what it means for everyone involved.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h1: The Treasury Node on Mainnet: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Contract
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.p1: Most "non-custodial" claims in this industry are a policy: a team says it won't move your funds, and you decide whether to believe them. Ours is a constraint enforced by a smart contract we don't control. This post walks through one real transaction that proves it, and what that proof is worth to everyone standing near it - DeFindex, Etherfuse, OtterSec, the Stellar ecosystem, the people who'd eventually trust an agent with real money, and Nirium itself.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.p2: Nothing here is a summary you have to take on faith. Every hash, contract address, and line of code below is a link - go check it.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p1: On August 6, 2026 at 00:56:39 UTC, an address controlled by Nirium's agent called `rebalance()` on a live DeFindex vault on Stellar mainnet, with an `Invest` instruction, moving 1.0 CETES from the vault's idle balance into DeFindex's Etherfuse strategy. No human clicked anything. Transaction:
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p2: The address that signed this specific transaction has since rotated to a new key - routine operational hygiene, not a scandal. The vault's current RebalanceManager is itself a public, on-chain fact, readable by anyone by calling the vault's own `get_rebalance_manager()` view function - nothing about who holds this role is hidden behind our word.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p3: Here's the part that actually matters: this isn't a policy Nirium chose to follow. It's what the vault contract's own code allows the RebalanceManager role to do, full stop. `rebalance()` accepts four instructions - `Unwind`, `Invest`, `SwapExactIn` and `SwapExactOut` - and none of them takes a destination address as an argument. (Corrected 12 Nov 2026: this post first said two; Nirium's own code only sends `Invest` and `Unwind`, but the role also allows the two swaps, whose output always goes back to the vault.) `Unwind` hardcodes the destination to `e.current_contract_address()`, the vault itself; `Invest` has no destination parameter at all, funds only ever move into a strategy the vault already trusts. Withdrawing to an arbitrary address isn't blocked by a check somewhere - there's no code path that accepts one. The real worst case with a leaked agent key is a swap at a bad price inside the vault, losing value to slippage. Every other real capability - pausing a strategy, rescuing funds, changing which address holds a role - belongs to the Manager, a role Nirium's agent does not hold.

treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.evidence_source_label: The exact source code - rebalance(), Unwind and Invest

treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h_why: Why this matters, beyond this one transaction
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.why_p1: "We don't custody your funds" is the most common sentence in DeFi, and by itself it's worth nothing - it's exactly what a team about to run off with your money would also say. What changes the calculus isn't the sentence, it's whether the claim is checkable by someone with no reason to trust you. A contract's source code is checkable. A team's intentions are not.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.why_p2: That's the actual shift this transaction demonstrates: from "trust us" to "here's the code, here's the transaction, go verify both yourself." The agent doesn't hold the role that could take custody - DeFindex's Manager role does, and on this vault that role sits with the vault owner's key, separate from the agent's key. Today that owner is our own team (a self-funded test vault), so this proves the mechanism, not client custody. The agent proposes and executes rebalancing; it structurally cannot walk away with the money.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h_impact: What this means, actor by actor
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_intro: This isn't one story - it's a different, specific claim for each party near it, and none of them are ours to make unilaterally. Here's what each one can actually check.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_defindex_p: A vault architecture is only as strong as its worst integration. This is a real third party - not DeFindex's own documentation, not a synthetic test - putting real value through the RebalanceManager role exactly as designed, on mainnet, with the outcome publicly verifiable. That's a harder validation than any internal test suite can produce, and it's evidence DeFindex can point to, not just claim.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_etherfuse_p: CETES on Stellar just gained one more real, automated, and now-verified path into it - capital moving into the Etherfuse Blend strategy without a human at a terminal, and without anyone having to trust the party operating that automation. That's a concrete answer to the question every potential integrator asks before connecting to a yield product: what happens if the thing sending me capital gets compromised? Here: nothing it isn't allowed to do, because the contract won't let it.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_ottersec_p: An audit report proves code was reviewed. A real transaction, months later, behaving exactly the way that audited code says it should, is one more real data point that the contract behaves as documented, under an integration nobody wrote to pass a test. What the audit covered is OtterSec's to say, not ours.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_stellar_p: Non-custodial DeFi automation is a common pitch and a rare mainnet artifact. This is one concrete, dated, on-chain example of an autonomous agent moving real value between DeFi primitives on Stellar without ever holding custody of it - not a roadmap slide, not a testnet demo, a transaction anyone can decode themselves.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_h: For the people who'd eventually trust an agent with real money
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_p: To be direct about where this stands today: the vault in this post is Nirium's own team proving the mechanism with its own funds, not an outside client's money yet - worth saying plainly, since the whole point of this post is not overstating what's verifiable. What it gives a future client isn't a promise that it'll work when it's their turn. It's something to check before they ever have to take our word for anything: the exact contract, the exact role, the exact transaction, all public, all today.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_nirium_p: This is the kind of evidence that doesn't inflate under scrutiny - it's stronger the harder someone looks at it, which is the opposite of most claims made in this space. For the Stellar Community Fund and for any future partner evaluating whether the non-custodial claim is real, this transaction and the three lines of contract code behind it are the actual differentiator, not a line in a pitch deck.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.regulatory_map_p: One more thing: each party near this flow answers for its own activity under its own rules - Circle for USDC, Etherfuse for its tokenized CETES, DeFindex for its contracts. Their regulatory status is theirs to state; ask them, not us.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Every link above resolves to something you don't have to take our word for - a live block explorer, a public GitHub repository, a documentation page DeFindex controls, not us. Decode the transaction. Read the contract. If something here doesn't hold up the way this post says it does, that's worth knowing - for you and for us.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.where_body: Nirium's Treasury Node runs on mainnet as the RebalanceManager on a DeFindex vault structured so a client would own it - invite-only pending a written legal opinion on a specific open question under Mexico's anti-money-laundering law (LFPIORPI art. 17 fraction XVI, as Art. 24 Bis 4 of its General Rules defines it) on virtual-asset intermediation, with a public, client-signed path (propose-and-sign) available to anyone today. x402 settles on both testnet and mainnet (latest mainnet settlement: 18 Nov 2026), and audit anchoring runs on both. Correction (20 Oct 2026): an earlier version of this post said MPP was live on mainnet. MPP Charge is verified on testnet only. Treasury rebalancing has run on mainnet 4 times, on 6 Aug 2026, with the team's own funds - today's vault is our own team's, self-funded, not an outside client's yet. Corrected 16 Nov 2026: this post described Etherfuse's and Circle's regulatory status, said this flow converts USDC to CETES, and called the transaction 'audited and confirmed in production'. Those passages were removed or reworded: we had not verified the third-party regulatory claims ourselves, the vault holds one asset and does not convert, and what an audit covered is the auditor's to say.

x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.title: Mainnet x402 Was Down for 32 Days: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Fix
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Every paid mainnet request against Nirium's x402 endpoints failed for 32 days - not from our code, but from a stale RPC URL inside a facilitator we don't operate. Here's the root cause, the two independent real payments that prove it's fixed, and the permanent logging hook we shipped so the next one doesn't take a month to notice.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h1: Mainnet x402 Was Down for 32 Days: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Fix
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.p1: Every payment product built on a standard it doesn't fully control eventually meets the same test: what happens when the thing you depend on breaks, and it isn't your code? For 32 days, mainnet x402 payments against Nirium's endpoints failed on every attempt - not from a bug we wrote, but from a misconfiguration inside a facilitator we don't operate and can't patch ourselves. This post is the arc end to end: what broke, how we proved it wasn't ours, how it got fixed, and what we shipped so the next outage doesn't need an outside report to be noticed.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.p2: Nothing here is a summary you have to take on faith. Every transaction hash, GitHub comment, and file below is a link - go check it.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p1: Starting around August 10, 2026, every mainnet x402 settlement against Nirium's paid endpoints - and against every other integrator using the same hosted facilitator - began failing with `unexpected_verify_error`, a catch-all for an unhandled exception inside the facilitator's own `verify()` call. Not a rejected payment: the facilitator never got far enough to evaluate one. Isolation testing that day, and every day after, showed the same pattern: the identical client and payload settled cleanly on testnet, and failed the same way on mainnet, every single time.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p2: We filed OpenZeppelin/relayer-plugin-x402-facilitator#47 on August 19. Three independent integrators - us, AgentLedger, and a third party - converged on the exact same finding across a month of silence on two official OpenZeppelin channels. What actually broke it open wasn't the thread or a support-forum post: it was tagging, by handle and directly, the two maintainers we'd verified were still active elsewhere in the org. One replied within a day.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p3: The root cause, once posted: the hosted pubnet facilitator instance was pointed at a stale RPC URL, so `verify()` threw before it ever reached the payload. We retested the same afternoon with a real settlement against our own mainnet endpoint - clean `200`, confirmed on Horizon. A second, fully independent team ran the identical test the next day, with the same result. Two teams, two payments, two different days, one root cause:
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.evidence_tx2_label: AgentLedger's confirmation, next day (an integration test from a wallet Nirium's founder funded)
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.evidence_issue_label: The issue we filed - now closed
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.evidence_devlog_label: Our own devlog entry, dates and all
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h_why: Why this matters, beyond this one outage
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.why_p1: Every payment product built on x402 - ours included - depends on a facilitator it doesn't operate. That dependency is real, not theoretical, and pretending otherwise doesn't make an outage less likely. What actually changes the outcome is whether the failure gets found, diagnosed with the same discipline as a bug in your own code, and made visible instead of quietly retried into invisibility.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.why_p2: The right response to depending on infrastructure you don't control isn't to hide when it breaks - it's to instrument it, diagnose it with method, and leave permanent visibility behind so the next failure doesn't need an outside report to be noticed.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h_impact: What this means, actor by actor
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_intro: This isn't one story - it's a different, specific claim for each party near it. Here's what each one can actually check.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_openzeppelin_p: A hosted facilitator carries real operational weight - every integrator's paid traffic routes through it, and a silent misconfiguration on their side is invisible from ours until someone reports it from outside. Once tagged directly, the actual fix (correcting the pubnet RPC URL) landed within two days, and it's held under two independent teams' real settlements since. That outcome matters more than how long the silence lasted.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_fernando_p: His own mainnet payment hit this exact outage on September 4, blocked by something entirely outside his control or ours. He stayed in the thread, retried the day after the fix shipped, and posted his own confirmation - a second real settlement, from a second account, with the same clean result.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_stellar_p: This ran entirely on mainnet, against real infrastructure, with real fee-sponsored USDC settlements - not a testnet demo standing in for one. A facilitator outage affecting a whole ecosystem is exactly the kind of failure that's easy to describe in the abstract and hard to prove was real; this post exists so nobody has to take that part on faith either.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_p: The mainnet paid path is reliable again, confirmed by two separate teams on two separate days - not just our own word that it's fixed. Nothing changes on the integration side: the same client, the same endpoints, the same header. If it failed for you during this window, it wasn't your integration.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_nirium_p: We shipped a server-side logging hook mid-outage - `onAfterVerify`/`onVerifyFailure` on the facilitator client, writing every rejection reason and payer address into our own logs instead of only being visible from outside. It stays in place permanently, not as a workaround for this specific bug: it's the difference between finding the next facilitator regression ourselves and waiting for another integrator to report it first.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Every link above resolves to something you don't have to take our word for - a live block explorer, a GitHub issue thread, our own devlog entry with the dates and root cause spelled out. Decode the transactions. Read the thread. If something here doesn't hold up the way this post says it does, that's worth knowing - for you and for us.

execution.title: 1. Autonomous rebalancing (Treasury)
execution.content: If you enable autonomous rebalancing, you name Nirium's agent as the RebalanceManager of your own DeFindex vault. It can still act at a bad moment: the agent can decide wrongly, run late or stop, and the nodes that run it can go down. Someone who obtained the agent's key could move funds between your vault and its strategies, or swap inside the vault (the role allows it; Nirium's code never sends one), and lose value to slippage, but never take funds out of the vault. On mainnet this is invite-only, and so is deploying or funding a vault from this site; withdrawing from a vault you already own is never restricted.

contracts.title: 2. Smart contracts and third-party protocols
contracts.content: Vaults are DeFindex contracts, and their strategies lend through Blend. Both have third-party audits (DeFindex by OtterSec, March 2025), but an audit does not remove risk and does not cover each vault's configuration. Taking funds out of a lending strategy depends on that pool having enough liquidity at that moment. Nirium's own contracts (NiriumVault, NiriumProtocol) are not audited and run on testnet only.

hero.title: Treasury Node
hero.subtitle: Moves your vault's idle funds (USDC or CETES) into its Blend strategy and back when the yield crosses the thresholds you set. The vault is yours; Nirium only holds the role that rebalances inside it.
hero.invite_note: On mainnet, autonomous rebalancing and deploying or funding a vault from this site or the API are invite-only until we have a written legal opinion. On testnet everything is open.

step1.title: Measures the real yield
step1.body: Every 10 minutes the agent reads your vault on-chain and measures what the money actually earned: how much each vault share is worth over time. Until it has that history for a vault, it falls back to the fixed CETES reference rate, and the log says which of the two it used.

step2.title: You set two thresholds
step2.body: An entry rate and an exit rate (2.5% and 2.0% by default), plus a minimum amount below which nothing moves. Between the two thresholds the agent stays still, so it does not pay fees going in and out.

step3.title: The agent signs inside your vault
step3.body: When the yield crosses a threshold, the agent signs Invest or Unwind with its own key. Those calls only move money between the vault and its strategy: they take no destination address, so nothing can leave the vault.

step4.title: Settles on Stellar
step4.body: Each move is a Stellar transaction, final in seconds. Deposits and withdrawals are signed by you, with your own wallet. Nirium never holds your funds.

step5.title: Anyone can check it
step5.body: Every move is a public transaction anyone can look up. To date on mainnet: 4 rebalances of a vault holding CETES, with our own funds, all on 6 Aug 2026, none since.
